halide:pldi:2013:
The wider citing literature engages the paper along two paths — through the compiler, and through the idea of separating an algorithm from its schedule — and the idea traveled further. TVM carried the compute/schedule separation into deep-learning compilation and became a lineage of its own — a meaningful share of the citations reach Halide only as TVM's ancestor — while T2S-Tensor and HeteroCL adapted the model to spatial hardware and FPGAs, and TACO's scheduling language generalized it to sparse iteration spaces. The compiler itself became shared research infrastructure: the automatic-scheduling literature, from tree-search and beam-search schedulers to Monte-Carlo tuners, treats Halide as its standard substrate, and verification work has targeted both its compiler and its scheduling rewrites.

Beyond research descendants, Halide pipelines run in production imaging systems — synthetic depth-of-field on mobile phones among them — and imaging-DSP toolchains extend the compiler toward their own targets. The remaining citation mass is the signature of an idea that became vocabulary: several hundred works cite the paper as one item in lists of domain-specific compilers, or with a single sentence crediting the origin of the algorithm/schedule separation, without engaging the system itself.
thies:cc:2002:
Beyond the project, the citing literature engaged both halves of the work. The compiler and its programs served as infrastructure across the field: sketching-based synthesis took bit-streaming StreamIt programs as its input domain, and a line of mapping work — partitioning streaming parallelism for multicores, software-pipelined execution on GPUs, Flextream's adaptive compilation, Sponge, and Optimus's synthesis to FPGAs — compiled or scheduled StreamIt programs onto nearly every parallel substrate of its era. Several manycore projects adopted the language outright as their input format.

The paper's most distinctive afterlife belongs to its benchmark suite. Dozens of evaluations across compilers and architectures run on the StreamIt benchmarks — often through the STR2RTS refactoring, itself a paper about the suite — so the workloads outlived the compiler as the streaming community's shared reference set. In the surrounding literature the language appears as the canonical member of lists of streaming languages, alongside the dataflow work it descends from.
taylor:micro:2002:
In the wider literature Raw stands as the exemplar of the tiled microprocessor. Much of its influence is routed through descendants — the tiled-microprocessor line that followed it and the commercial many-core designs it led to — so a portion of the citing literature engages Raw's ideas through successor machines rather than the original. The fabricated chip also had a working life of its own: a 1020-node microphone-array beamformer, software-based instruction caching, and stream-algorithm studies used the Raw machine as their platform.

A second, quieter pattern runs through the architecture literature: individual measurements from this paper became standing evidence. The fraction of chip resources consumed by the interconnect and the latencies of the scalar operand network are cited across a long line of network-on-chip papers as the motivating numbers for their designs. Beyond that, the paper appears wherever tiled architectures are enumerated — a fixture of the related-work paragraph that places any spatial architecture in context.
amarasinghe:ijpp:2005: The citing literature treats the article mainly as a point of reference for the StreamIt model: streaming systems describe it and set their own designs against it, with StreamPI among those that compare directly, and it appears as a member of the standard list of streaming languages. A smaller number of works reuse its kernels in their evaluations or borrow its design rationale for other domains. Its reception largely mirrors, at smaller scale, that of the conference paper it expands.
petkov:ipdps:2002: In the citing literature the transformation survives as a name: works reference unroll-and-squash itself, usually in a sentence crediting it as a way to pipeline loops under resource constraints. The high-level-synthesis literature on loop pipelining places it among the transformations it builds past, and signal-processing implementations on FPGAs apply it to their kernels. The record is nearly all differentiation and technique credit rather than reuse of an artifact — the reception of a transformation that entered the compiler vocabulary and is engaged wherever loop pipelining is surveyed.
thies:toplas:2007: The step was taken up. The storage-optimization literature treats the affine unified occupancy vector as a formal object to build on: the lattice-based memory-allocation line generalized it explicitly — extended lattice-based allocation subsumes occupancy vectors among its unified inputs — and the intra-array storage-optimization work that followed positions its contributions against this framework. Its ideas also reappear in polyhedral treatments of sparse code generation. The citations are few and concentrated in one community, but almost all of them are substantive: this is a paper cited by the people extending its mathematics.
levison:istas:2002: Later work cites TEK as a predecessor system in the line of research on web access under constrained connectivity. The ICT-for-development systems that followed — RuralCafe, COCO, Samvidha, and low-bandwidth search designs among them — describe its asynchronous, email-carried search model and position their own architectures against it, and the paper appears in broader accounts of rural networking and the digital divide as an early example of designing services for intermittent connections. The citation record is small and specific: nearly every citing work is itself a system in the same problem space.
netblocks-pldi24: External citations are substantive rather than incidental: work on RPC communication for microservices builds on its staged approach to custom host network stacks, and the staged-programming and network-function literatures name it among the systems that generate specialized packet-processing code. The pattern, at small scale, is descent rather than mention: the works that cite it are the ones building on it.
ansel:pact:2014:
Outside the group the framework found the use it was designed for: research systems across several domains embed it as their search engine. PolyMage tunes its image-pipeline schedules with it; the Lift stencil-code generator and the verified-lifting work of Kamil and colleagues drive their searches through it; ApproxHPVM and ApproxTuner use it to navigate accuracy-performance tradeoffs; and FPGA-oriented projects, from Cong's composable accelerator generation to LAMDA, either run it directly or extend its technique ensemble. Uses stretch as far as tuning JPEG quantization for classification networks and Singh and Solar-Lezama's generation of formula simplifiers.

A comparable share of the citing literature meets the paper from the other side, as a measuring stick: new autotuners evaluate themselves against its bandit ensemble or position their designs relative to it. Beyond these engaged citations lies a broad peripheral mass that names OpenTuner as the standard example of a general-purpose autotuning framework, a sign that the name settled into the field's shared vocabulary.
gordon:asplos:2002: Beyond the thesis, external reception runs largely through StreamIt itself: groups retargeting the language treat this paper's partitioning, layout, and communication scheduling as the reference compilation path. Huynh and colleagues mapped streaming applications onto multi-GPU systems, Wang and O'Boyle partitioned stream graphs with machine learning, and StreamX10 carried the approach to X10, while work on throughput-driven synthesis for pipelined multicores measured against it. The larger citation mass is more distant: the paper appears in many works as the example of compiling a stream language onto communication-exposed hardware, and a steady share cites its Raw results as evidence of what static orchestration can achieve.
graphit: Where the citing literature engages GraphIt, it is mainly as a performance bar. Hardware and accelerator papers measure against its generated code — GraphLily on FPGAs, Capstan for sparsity, work on SpMV-based graph processing — and architecture studies such as Pipette and Dalorex run its programs as workloads, while a GAP-suite evaluation of graph frameworks includes it among those compared. A smaller thread engages the compiler itself, as GraphAttack and Grafs do, and Allo carries the algorithm/schedule separation into accelerator design. Most of the remaining citations are lighter, naming GraphIt among the systems a paper lists or differentiates itself from.
babb:fccm:1999: The citing literature received the work mostly as a marker. Its main afterlife is in surveys of reconfigurable computing — Compton and Hauck, Todman and colleagues, Tessier's surveys of the field — where the compiler stands as an example of carrying sequential C and Fortran all the way to hardware. Engaged citations are few: the DIVA processing-in-memory work differentiates its architecture against this approach, and Rugina and Rinard's work on pointer analysis for structured parallel programs made use of the compiler. Most other citations name the paper in passing while mapping the space of C-to-gates compilation, so the reception is modest in depth if not in venue.
gottschlich:mapl:2018: The vocabulary is what circulated. Citing papers rarely engage the taxonomy in depth; instead they invoke it to locate their own work within machine programming, and they come from the breadth the paper called for — learned database systems such as Bao and RadixSpline, neural-network verification, program synthesis, even the inference of chemical procedures from text. Nearly all of these citations are peripheral: the paper is cited for its framing, as position papers are, its three-pillar scheme serving as shorthand for a research agenda rather than as a technique anyone extends.
lee:micro:2002: Reception outside that toolchain is compact but concrete. The most sustained take-up is a transplant: Baraglia, Capannini, and colleagues carried the confidence-weighted, multi-pass design into job scheduling for large computing farms, first adopting the idea and then extending it into a multi-criteria framework, while Win and Wong applied the cooperative-pass approach to instruction scheduling with linear-scan register allocation. Within spatial-architecture compilation the paper is mostly a point of reference: the EDGE static-placement work measures against it, and modulo-scheduling papers for coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures position their schedulers relative to it. The remainder cites it in passing among spatial scheduling techniques.
maydan:lcpc:1992: The citation record reflects that supersession: the workshop version is cited sparsely, and mostly in passing. The most visible thread is the runtime-parallelization line of Rauchwerger and Padua, whose LRPD-test papers list it among the compile-time analyses their speculative approach sidesteps; surveys of automatic parallelization place it alongside its contemporaries, and occasional works cite its treatment of array data-flow as supporting evidence. One later effort on accurate array data-flow analysis engages the mathematics directly. A fair share of the record is unjudged, but what has been examined suggests a paper read chiefly through its POPL successor.
stephenson:eurogp:2003: With the PLDI paper absorbing the primary citations, the EuroGP version's own record is small and lives where it was addressed: the evolutionary-computation literature cites it as the compiler example. Harman's survey of search-based software engineering, Burke and colleagues' treatment of hyper-heuristics, and a survey of compiler autotuning using machine learning all place it among applications of genetic programming, while papers on genetic instruction scheduling and on optimization-space exploration position their approaches near it. Few citations dig into the evolved priority functions themselves; the paper is received as an instance of an idea rather than as an artifact.
asplos013: The citing literature is small but comes from the community the work targets. Distributed stream-processing systems treat Gloss as a design point to differentiate from: Megaphone and Meces, both concerned with reconfiguring running dataflows, position their state-migration designs against it. The self-adaptation line of Vogel, Griebler, and colleagues cites its results as evidence, in a systematic review of self-adaptation for parallel stream processing and in work on transparent adaptation of stream parallel patterns. The remaining citations are passing mentions in papers on rescaling and elasticity — a modest record, concentrated where live reconfiguration is actually studied.
amarasinghe:cgo:2005: What traveled is the argument rather than any artifact. The small citing literature invokes the keynote almost entirely as evidence: the pipeline-parallelism line of Giacomoni, Vachharajani, and colleagues, from FastForward through its companion reports, cites it for the premise that multicores shift the burden of performance onto software, and work on visualizing potential parallelism and on teaching multicore programming uses it the same way. Every judged citation is peripheral, and none builds on the talk itself — the expected shape for a keynote abstract whose diagnosis was becoming common ground.
seq-nature-biotech: Reception of the correspondence itself is small but concrete. The citations that engage it come from tools: a framework for characterizing segmental duplication structure across genome assemblies is written in Seq, Sequre builds secure multiparty computation for biomedical data sharing on top of it, and Vectron uses its infrastructure for auto-vectorized dynamic programming. Other genomics work, including minimizer-space assembly and the mapquik read mapper, cites it when arguing that performance-minded tooling matters in the field. Much of the small external record is unjudged, so the fuller picture is uncertain, but the judged citations are the kind a language wants: people writing software in it.
ansel:gecco:2011: Outside those descendants, external reception is thin. The most substantive notice comes from the autotuning community itself: Basu, Hall, and colleagues discuss the algorithm in their account of making autotuning mainstream, treating it as one of the field's evolutionary search strategies. Later tuners such as Bliss, and work on parallel iterative compilation, cite it only in passing. The paper's reception is hard to separate from the PetaBricks project it served; read on its own, it is a technique noted by close neighbors rather than one taken up beyond them.
bruening:cgo:2003:
Beyond that lineage, the deepest external engagement comes from people who ran the system rather than merely cited it. Tool-building citations range across security, performance analysis, and software maintenance: Ruwase and Lam built their practical dynamic buffer overflow detector on DynamoRIO; helper-threaded prefetching on the Sun UltraSPARC CMP, online impact analysis via dynamic compilation, studies of bounded code caches, live detection and repair of false sharing, and software wear management for persistent memories all used it as their instrumentation substrate; and JIT instrumentation carried its approach into operating-system kernels. The users span the paper's own decade through to memory-access-pattern classification work at ASPLOS years later.

The larger mass of citations is thinner. In surveys and related-work sections DynamoRIO serves as a customary example of dynamic binary translation, named alongside other frameworks rather than engaged in detail, and a further group measures new systems against it or positions instrumentation designs relative to it. The record thus has two layers: a broad backdrop of brief mentions, and a steady core of substantive users for whom the infrastructure promise of the title was kept.
tiramisu: That turn toward learned optimization shaped the reception. The deepest external engagement uses Tiramisu as a research vehicle for machine-learning-driven compilation: Pearl's deep-reinforcement-learning optimizer, an experimental study of LLM-guided loop optimization, pre-trained performance models, the LOOPerSet dataset, and CHEHAB RL for homomorphic encryption all run on the compiler, and its affine machinery was carried into quantum circuit mapping; further afield, the CoRa tensor compiler used it in its work on ragged tensors. The much larger share of citations is list membership: across the tensor-compiler and scheduling-language literature, Tiramisu appears alongside other polyhedral and scheduling-language systems as a point on the map rather than a system engaged in detail.
thies:pact:2010: In the citing literature the study leads a double life, as evidence and as workloads. Its findings — above all that most filters are stateless — are cited to support design decisions in later streaming languages, runtimes, and schedulers, and the characterized suite itself became a source of evaluation workloads across the embedded-systems literature: hard-real-time scheduling of streaming applications, energy-efficient mapping onto MPSoCs, NoC and CGRA design, and machine-learned partitioning of streaming programs all draw benchmarks from it, and the Savina actor benchmark suite draws on it as well. Few works extend the study itself; its role is to be the empirical ground other designs stand on.
ding:pldi:2015: The citing literature treats the paper mainly as an example. Surveys of compiler autotuning using machine learning, overviews of machine learning in compiler optimization, and accounts of autotuning in high-performance computing cite it as an instance of input-adaptive tuning, and most other references are brief. A smaller group takes up the problem itself: a pattern-based algorithmic autotuner for graph processing on GPUs adopts input-aware algorithmic choice, empirical work on input-aware performance models of configurable systems builds on the framing, and White-Box Program Tuning measures against it. The reception, in short, registers the paper as the marker for input sensitivity in autotuning rather than as a system others run.
senanayake2020sparse: The uptake runs deepest inside the sparse-compilation community. Mosaic builds its interoperable tensor-algebra compiler on the framework, Stardust extends it toward reconfigurable dataflow hardware, the compilation of modular and general sparse workspaces continues the workspaces line, and the Sparse Abstract Machine, DISTAL, and a compiler for fused relational operations on multisets carry its ideas elsewhere. Others use it as a measuring stick: polyhedral code generation for sparse contraction and register tiling for unstructured sparsity compare against it, and BaCO tunes over its scheduling space. The remaining citations mostly place the paper in lists of sparse tensor compilers, so the record is compact but substantive at its center.
zhao:cgo:2010: External users followed the same pattern, building tools on Umbra rather than writing about it: comprehensive kernel instrumentation via dynamic binary translation, the MINIME benchmark synthesizer, the Taint Rabbit's optimized taint analysis, and machine-learned detection of parallel patterns all employ its shadow-memory framework. Neighboring designs engage it as a reference point — the case for unlimited watchpoints measures against it, and AddressSanitizer positions its own shadow scheme relative to Umbra's translation. The rest of the record is brief: dynamic-analysis papers list Umbra among memory-shadowing systems. The citations are not many, but the most substantive of them come from people who used the framework.
falsesharing:sc:2013: Reception splits along the paper's two identities. The false-sharing detectors that followed — PREDATOR, Cheetah, LASER, Featherlight — cite it chiefly to differentiate their own approaches, contrasting precise memory-level analysis with its performance-event classification. The machine-learning identity found a more direct successor: the zero-positive learning line, from diagnosing software performance regressions through AutoPerf and AutoCon, treats it as the baseline for learned detection of performance anomalies, and DR-BW lists it among precedents for supervised learning over hardware counters. Beyond these two threads the citations are brief mentions, and the record as a whole is modest and concentrated in the performance-tools community.
jaeyeon:asplos:2023: That framing — format and schedule tuned as one — is what the citing literature takes from the paper. Subsequent sparse-tensor autotuners measure themselves against WACO: AutoSparse, RASSM, UniSparTa, and SparseZETA use it as a baseline, STile differentiates its hybrid-format search from it, and COGNATE extends the approach with transfer learning toward emerging hardware. Outside that circle the citations are brief, listing WACO among learned approaches to sparse computation. The record is small but pointed: most of its substantive citations come from systems competing on exactly the problem the paper posed.
looplets-cgo23: External engagement stays close to home. The citation record is small and concentrated in the sparse- and structured-array-compilation community: Galley builds its query optimizer for sparse tensor programs over the abstraction, the compilation of shape operators on sparse arrays and work on load-balanced partitioning of unstructured sparse tensor algebra use it, a mechanized algebra of verified data structures adopts its approach to structure, and work on compressing structured tensor algebra defines itself against it. Beyond that circle the paper appears in a chronology of scheduling languages and in compiler lists. The audience is narrow, but the works at its center engage the language itself.
sheldon:lcpc:2001: The external record is thin, and much of it unjudged, but the audience it found is a particular one: hardware synthesis. Devos's work on loop transformations for the optimized generation of reconfigurable hardware builds directly on the techniques, and the optimizations are cited in FPGA design methodology using streaming, in expression synthesis for process networks generated by LAURA, and in constructing application-specific memory hierarchies on FPGAs — settings where array transformations introduce exactly the divisions and modulos the paper eliminates. A later treatment of modulo-based array indexing in loops positions itself against the approach, evidence that the problem, if narrow, kept its relevance.
tiramisu-li: The citation record is thin and uniformly brief. The paper appears in passing, mostly in the related work of later efforts in the same line — Pearl's reinforcement-learning code optimization, cost models supporting dynamic program sizes, a reinforcement-learning environment for the MLIR compiler, CHEHAB's homomorphic-encryption optimization — and in a survey of lightweight deep learning, as one instance of a learned compiler heuristic. No citing work engages the model in depth; its reception is as an entry in the catalogue of neural approaches to loop optimization.
buildsl-cgo22: Outside those two lines the citation record is thin. A few external works cite the paper briefly: a systematic literature review of DSLs for algorithmic graph processing includes it, eCC++ names it as an instance of compiler construction for embedded DSLs, and Flan's Datalog compiler mentions it in passing among staging-based systems. None engages the staging argument in depth; the case the paper makes is carried mainly by the group's own successor systems rather than by external uptake.
gordon:asplos:2006:
Beyond those descendants, the citing literature engaged the paper on a large scale, though mostly at a distance: multicore-compilation and parallel-language papers cite its findings — that applications differ in their dominant form of parallelism, and that a compiler can exploit all three forms together — as evidence, position their own mappers against its approach, or place it in surveys and lists of stream-compilation work. A substantial engaged band works with it concretely.

The most direct successors treat it as the baseline for stream partitioning: Wang and O'Boyle's partitioning streaming parallelism for multi-cores and their later machine-learning partitioner measure against its heuristics. Its StreamIt benchmarks travel too, into mapping stream programs onto heterogeneous multiprocessor systems and an evaluation of dynamic voltage and frequency scaling for stream programs, while Liquid Metal and adaptive input-aware compilation for graphics engines build with the compiler, and compiler techniques for massively scalable implicit task parallelism carry its ideas into task-parallel settings.
kiriansky:security:2002: In the wider literature the paper serves as a common point of reference for execution monitoring: later defenses position their mechanisms against shepherding's policies, surveys of software security carry it forward, and a long tail cites it briefly among prior work. The closer engagements run through the infrastructure as much as the idea. Systems such as comprehensive kernel instrumentation via dynamic binary translation, PiPA, BlackBox, and work on binary compatibility for SGX enclaves build on the shepherding implementation and its DynamoRIO descendants, while a few works — securing the kernel via static binary rewriting and program shepherding, and the LAIDS/LIDS framework for systematic IPS design — take up the idea itself.
chou:2018:formats: Outside the project, the level-format abstraction became a shared vocabulary for sparse compilation. Works that adopt the idea carry it beyond taco's setting: the Sparse Abstract Machine builds a hardware abstraction around per-dimension level formats, Stardust and SpDISTAL take the approach to reconfigurable dataflow and distributed machines, and compiler work on modular sparse workspaces and sparse tensor convolutions reasons in the same terms. Others use taco itself, from GPU code generation in Sgap to query optimization in Galley. Around this core, a larger body of sparse-systems papers cites the work, often in passing, as one of the compilers that made formats a first-class concern.
palkar:vldb:2018: The citing literature treats the paper mainly as a reference for what end-to-end optimization across data-science libraries can achieve: papers on query compilation and analytics systems cite Weld, usually briefly, when motivating or classifying their own designs. A smaller band engages the system directly. Willump builds its machine-learning inference optimizer on Weld; Tuplex and later work on declarative sub-operators measure against it as the composable-optimization baseline; PyTond reuses its data-science workloads; and the split-annotations work on optimizing data-intensive computations in existing libraries returns to the same benchmarks. The reception is concentrated in the database-systems community that the paper addressed.
amin:iccd:2009: The reception sits almost entirely in the microfluidic design-automation literature that formed around flow-based chips in the following decade. Control-layer synthesis work — control synthesis for flow-based microfluidic large-scale integration biochips, control-layer routing and control-pin minimization, integrated flow-control codesign — treats the paper's control-line minimization and valve-routing algorithms as an early formulation to refine or generalize, and its discussions of the paper are often detailed rather than perfunctory. Micado itself found users: Fluigi builds on it, and work on automatic synthesis of microfluidic chips from a domain-specific language employs it. The remaining citations place the paper among the origins of CAD for mVLSI biochips.
chen:asplos:2021: Among citing works VeGen figures chiefly as a marker in the vectorization literature: papers on tensor compilers and SIMD code generation list it among approaches that reach beyond packed SIMD, usually in a sentence or two. The substantive engagement comes from synthesis-based vectorizers and instruction-selection work — Coyote, vector instruction selection for digital signal processors using program synthesis, Minotaur, and Hydride — which position their techniques against VeGen's generation of a vectorizer from instruction semantics. The record is modest and skews toward brief mentions, but the works that do engage are those pursuing the same question of retargetable vector code generation.
goslp: External reception is modest and concentrated where one would expect, in the SLP vectorization literature. The line of SLP refinements from Porpodas and colleagues — VW-SLP and Super-Node SLP — positions its heuristics against goSLP's global ILP formulation, and Coyote does the same for vectorizing encrypted arithmetic circuits. Elsewhere the paper appears in lists of auto-vectorization work or as evidence about the state of SLP vectorizers; an evaluation of compilers' capability of automatic vectorization gives it a closer reading. The citations are few, but the substantive ones come from the community refining SLP itself.
zhao:wbia:2005: The citation record is thin and consists mostly of list membership: works on memory allocators, mobile systems, and data-center software cite the paper as one instance of dynamic memory optimization, typically in a sentence. The closer engagements are scattered. MMT, exploiting fine-grained parallelism in dynamic memory management, reuses its experimental setting, as does work on symbolic range analysis of pointers; Cling, a memory allocator to mitigate dangling pointers, discusses its context-based pooling in some detail. The paper circulates mainly as a named example of runtime pool allocation and prefetching rather than as a base that later systems build on.
olszewski:asplos:2012: The citing record is small but attentive: most of it comes from the data-race-detection literature, and an unusually large share of those works discuss the system in technical depth rather than in passing. IFRit measures against Aikido as a detector of comparable accuracy; OCTET and Kard, which builds lightweight race detection on per-thread memory protection, position their designs relative to its hypervisor-based approach; and proposals such as RADISH give its page-protection technique a detailed reading when arguing for their own mechanisms. Citation is confined to one community, but within it the paper is read as a serious design point for low-overhead sharing detection.
ugcf-isca21: External citation is sparse and clusters around the architectures UGC targets. Work in the HammerBlade line uses the compiler — the paper on supporting dynamic task parallelism on manycore architectures builds with it, and the HammerBlade manycore paper lists it among the software the machine runs — while compiler papers such as MeshTaichi, a multi-target multi-paradigm DSL compiler for algorithmic graph processing, and a tensor processing framework for CPU-manycore heterogeneous systems give it closer readings as a point of comparison for multi-backend design. A systematic literature review of graph-processing DSLs records it among the languages of the field.
ahrens_finch_2025: The citing record is small, but its closest reader extends the system. WingSpan builds concurrency and dependence analysis for sparse and structured tensor compilers on Finch, and the TENSURE work on fuzzing sparse tensor compilers treats it as a compiler to measure against. Work on compressing structured tensor algebra and on optimizing sparse tensor compilation for sparse output positions its own approach against Finch's handling of structure and control flow. The remaining mentions are brief placements among sparse tensor compilers.
thies:acm-sigarch-news:2002: Direct citation of the position paper is scant; the argument it distills belongs to the project's language and compiler papers, which carry the fuller treatment. Of the handful of external citations, one is substantive: work on disjoint-path routing for streaming applications works with the StreamIt infrastructure in the tiled-architecture setting the paper describes. Generating stream based code from plain C positions its recovery of streaming structure against StreamIt's explicit approach, and the rest are passing mentions. The paper's role is best read through the compiler line it argued for.
waingold:computer:1997:
Beyond that arc, the citing literature receives the article mostly as shorthand for a category of machines. Raw appears in surveys of on-chip parallelism and in the lists with which later architecture papers situate themselves, cited as the tiled design that hands wires, scheduling, and routing to the compiler; only a minority of the citations engage its mechanisms in detail. Papers proposing new architectures differentiate their choices from Raw's, and others draw on its arguments and measurements as evidence in debates over scaling and wire delay.

The deepest engagement stays close to the machine itself. Theses and companion papers within the project's orbit — software-based instruction caching, the SIFt streaming compiler, compilation to the exposed memory hierarchy, a Raw network router, and compiler support for scalable memory systems — treat the article as the definition of the platform they build on, and later Raw publications such as Versatile Tiled-Processor Architectures carry its description forward. Outside that circle the paper serves as a fixed point of reference: the design against which other tiled and configurable proposals explain themselves.
stephenson:pldi:2003: Beyond the thesis, the citing literature treats the paper as a reference point for machine-learned compiler heuristics. The most substantive engagement adopts the idea rather than the code: priority-function learning reappears in atomic block formation for explicit data graph execution architectures, in metaoptimization of inlining priority functions for TRIPS, in Cavazos and Moss's induced scheduling heuristics, and in machine-learning approaches to partitioning streaming parallelism for multi-cores. A larger mass of surveys and related-work sections cites the paper as an early demonstration of machine learning for compilers, and autotuning work differentiates its search strategies from the paper's genetic programming. Most citations are brief, but the substantive ones transplant the priority-function idea to new heuristics.
hall:sc:1995: Reception in the citing literature runs unusually deep for its size: a large share of the citations come from work that ran the compiler rather than merely naming it. SUIF Explorer built its interactive parallelization support on the system; compiler-directed page coloring drew its parallelized applications from it; and a line of work on software distributed shared memory by Han, Tseng, and Keleher used its output to study runtime support for compiler-parallelized codes. Later work extended the analysis toward coarse-grain pipelining on FPGAs, and predicated array data-flow analysis measured itself against the paper's results. The rest of the record largely cites the coverage figures as evidence of what interprocedural analysis can find.
ansel:pldi:2011: In the citing literature the paper stands as the reference for making sandboxes admit dynamically generated code. Security work on isolation and control-flow integrity cites it when marking that boundary: MiniBox and the control-flow-integrity papers of Niu and Tan note it as the extension of software-based fault isolation to JIT compilers, and the WebAssembly design paper lists it among the developments around Native Client. Engagement beyond positioning is thinner but concrete — the work on bringing Java's native code under control used its mechanisms directly, and Fay adopted its ideas for safe runtime instrumentation. Most other citations are brief mentions in surveys of sandboxing and memory-safety defenses.
taylor:isscc:2003: To the circuits community, meanwhile, the paper is the Raw chip's entry in the record of multicore silicon, and it is cited chiefly as an exemplar: papers on networks-on-chip and multiprocessor systems-on-chip list the design when surveying tiled interconnects, and low-power on-chip network work differentiates its choices from Raw's. The more engaged citations measure against the chip — the AsAP asynchronous processor array reports comparisons with it, and a performance analysis of PIM, stream, and tiled processing exercised it on memory-intensive signal-processing kernels — while the TILE64 paper discusses the design at length. The record is modest and mostly peripheral, consistent with an implementation paper whose ideas circulate through its companions.
zhao:cc:2008: EDDI's own citation record is modest and consists mostly of list membership: it appears in related-work sections of debugging, instrumentation, and tracing papers as the demonstration that software watchpoints can scale far beyond the hardware debug registers. A handful of works engage more directly — the work on lightweight memory tracing differentiates its design from EDDI's, and PinADX discusses it in detail — but no external system in the record builds on the tool itself. What circulates is the result: papers from time-travel debugging to undefined-value detection cite the million-watchpoint figure as the reference point for instrumentation-based monitoring at scale.
kiriansky:pact:2016: Reception lies less in other compilers than in computer architecture. Hardware proposals for irregular memory access cite milk as the software point of comparison: PHI differentiates its approach from milk's, täkō measures against it as a baseline, DX100 reuses its workloads, and a survey of sparse-matrix accelerators picks up the idea. Peripheral mentions cluster in the same territory — locality-enhancing systems from hardware-accelerated graph-traversal scheduling to SpMV vectorization list DRAM-conscious clustering among software answers to the random-access problem. The record is small but placed where the technique aimed: papers about making indirect references cheap.
chou-pldi20-taco-conversion: Within the sparse-compilation literature the work registers as part of taco's format story. Successor sparse compilers position themselves relative to it: SparseTIR and UniSparse treat the generated conversion routines as a point of departure or a baseline for format customization, and the MLIR sparse-tensor compiler discusses the approach in detail. The work on compiling modular and general sparse workspaces builds on the machinery directly, and papers across sparse linear algebra — from Gamma's sparse matrix multiplication to AlphaSparse's generated SpMV codes — cite the conversion measurements as evidence that format choice and conversion cost matter. The remaining citations are brief mentions in the tensor-compiler literature.
tiramisu-auto: Outside that direct line, external engagement is small and mostly glancing. The model appears in related-work sections of the tensor-program autotuning literature — TLP differentiates its cost model from it, and systems from PolyGym to multi-pass autotuning frameworks list it among learned cost models — but few external works engage its mechanics. The clearest continuation is the work on supporting dynamic program sizes in deep-learning cost models, which extends the model itself. The paper is cited, in short, as one instance of a broader direction: learned cost models inside compiler search.
zhao:ismm:2010: External reception is sparser and concentrated in the shadow-memory niche. AddressSanitizer differentiates its shadow mapping from EMS64's displacement scheme, and the PROMPT memory-profiling framework measures against it as a baseline; Skadu cites its results as evidence in its treatment of vector shadow memories, and papers on page overlays and Java metadata tracking list it among shadow-memory designs. The remaining citations are passing mentions. This is a technique cited by the small community that builds shadow-memory systems, mostly to situate their own mappings.
arxiv:2506.11021: The preprint's citation record is small and entirely peripheral. Such engagement as exists comes from work on estimating the correctness of generated code: papers on ensemble-based uncertainty estimation and on predicting program correctness by ensemble semantic entropy discuss the clustering approach in some detail, a paper on semantic collapse in coding models cites it as an example, and a study of optimal reasoning length for RL-trained language models takes up one of its ideas. Evaluations of hallucination in generative AI systems mention it in passing. This is reception at the registration stage: the method is noticed and named rather than built on.
thies:bmc:2007: Reception of the article is thin and lies outside the group's usual territory. CONCORD, a consensus method for secondary-structure prediction via mixed-integer linear optimization, engages it in detail; a later study of convolutional networks for secondary-structure prediction mentions it in passing; and work on structured prediction of matching and degree-constrained graphs cites it as an application of the underlying learning machinery. The few substantive mentions treat it as one entry among predictors that work without external databases — a contribution absorbed quietly into the secondary-structure literature rather than one that started a line.
hall:computer:1996:
In the citing literature the article serves as the standard reference for SUIF, and the largest single share of judged citations comes from work that used the compiler rather than merely naming it. SUIF Explorer grew an interactive, interprocedural parallelizer out of the same analyses; the work on superword-level parallelism in the presence of control flow built on the infrastructure; compiler frameworks for speculative multithreading, instruction generators for hybrid reconfigurable systems, and the Pace toolset for performance prediction took SUIF as their platform; and the machine-learning compilation line that begins with using machine learning to focus iterative optimization ran its studies through it.

A smaller body cites the results as evidence rather than infrastructure, invoking the NAS and SPECfp95 measurements as the mark of what interprocedural automatic parallelization achieves on shared-memory machines. The rest of the record is broad and shallow: the article named in lists of parallelizing compilers across architecture, language, and embedded-systems venues. That profile — a core of users inside a much larger ring of listings — is the reception of an infrastructure paper, cited by a community for the system it was running.
Ragan-Kelley:2017:HDA:3176926.3150211: Later work reaches this article as the accessible citation for Halide, and the judged record divides between a minority that engages the system or its central idea and a larger share that names Halide among schedule-based compilers and domain-specific languages. The engaged citations run the compiler — the synthetic depth-of-field pipeline for single-camera mobile phones among them — or carry the algorithm-schedule separation elsewhere: HeteroCL to software-defined reconfigurable computing, DISTAL and SWIRL to tensor-algebra and neural-network compilation, Exocompilation to hardware accelerators, automatic dataflow-graph partitioning to distributed deep learning. A portion of the citations reaches the paper through such successors, so part of its influence is routed through the lineage the idea created.
taylor:hpca:2003: Reception runs through the networks-on-chip literature, which absorbed the paper as the account of an extreme design point: on-chip networks whose latencies must be counted in single cycles. Citing works most often invoke its latency and occupancy measurements as evidence for how sensitive partitioned architectures are to operand transport, or place it in related-work discussions of on-chip interconnects; a few reuse its benchmarks. Deeper engagement is rarer. The sharing architecture builds on its ideas, a point-to-point inter-cluster network for clustered superscalar processors measures against it, and the account of the Tile Processor's on-chip interconnection architecture treats it in detail.
phothilimthana:asplos:2013: External readers cite the paper mostly as a marker in the CPU-GPU heterogeneous computing literature rather than as a system to build on. The ACM Computing Surveys treatment of CPU-GPU heterogeneous computing techniques includes it, and work on heterogeneous scheduling, data partitioning, and performance portability — the rewrite-rule generator of OpenCL code among them — names it as the autotuning point in the design space, sometimes pausing over the choice-and-poly-algorithm approach in detail. Direct reuse stays within the PetaBricks project itself; beyond it, the paper's role is that of a cited example of what installation-time autotuning across CPUs and GPUs can achieve.
Kjolstad:2017:TTG:3155562.3155683: Among citing works the tool paper serves as the citation for taco as an artifact, usually alongside the OOPSLA paper that supplies its theory. Its most common substantive role is as the system to measure against: the Capstan accelerator, SMASH, and a sparse tensor algebra compiler in MLIR take taco-generated kernels as their baseline, and SparseCore builds outward from it toward processor specialization for sparse computation. Others run the tool — SparseP, a closeness-centrality-based circuit partitioner for quantum simulations, CATBench as a compiler-autotuning benchmark — and Sparseloop carries its ideas into sparse accelerator modeling. The remainder is list membership among sparse tensor compilers.
zhang:dascmp:2007: Reception of the layer itself is modest and concentrated in the stream-compilation community. The substantive engagement came from Flextream, which used the framework in adaptive compilation of streaming applications for heterogeneous architectures, and from Streamware, which positions its own approach against it. Most other citations are brief: work on executing stream programs on GPUs, accelerators, and multiprocessor systems names the paper among StreamIt-based multicore backends when recounting how stream programs have been mapped to parallel hardware. The record is that of one system in a cluster of Cell-era streaming runtimes, cited together as a generation.
ahrens_autoscheduling_2022: The citation record is short and mostly glancing: sparse-compilation systems such as SparseTIR, the Sparse Abstract Machine, and Mosaic cite it in passing among schedulers and cost models for sparse code. The engaged citations, though, are the audience the paper addresses. SparseAuto adopts its ideas for auto-scheduling with recursive loop-nest restructuring, Galley builds on it for query optimization over sparse tensor programs, a fast autoscheduler for sparse machine-learning frameworks measures against it, and the indexed-streams formalization of fused contraction programs cites its results. With Looplets taking the protocolized notation as its input language, the paper sits at the base of a small line of asymptotic-cost scheduling work.
rawn:oopsla:2021: Beyond the group's own citing papers, external engagement is limited in volume but concentrated at the core: the paper's closest readers are builders. SpDISTAL carries the approach into distributed sparse tensor computation, the compilation of shape operators on sparse arrays extends the theory itself, FuseFlow applies it to sparse deep learning on streaming dataflow, and compilers for fused relational operations on multisets and for tensor-algebra representation of RTL simulation adopt its generalized sparse iteration. Around that core, SparseTIR and the MLIR sparse tensor work discuss it in detail, a polyhedral compiler for sparse tensor contraction measures against it, and the remaining citations are brief mentions in the sparse-compilation literature.
zhao:cgo:2007: Citation of UMI is sparse and mostly brief. The works that engage it sit in the online-profiling literature: RapidMRC and PiPA cite its results as evidence about the costs and feasibility of profiling memory behavior at runtime, and papers on cache-utility measurement and on automatic prefetching by binary rewriting position their designs against it. The rest is passing mention among lightweight profiling techniques, in work spanning full-system memory tracing, adaptive prefetching, and shared-cache management. The methodology registered in its community without, in the judged record, being adopted as a running system.
amarasinghe:siam:1995: Most of the works citing this overview have not been judged, so its reception can be read only in part. In the judged record the paper serves two roles: as a pointer to SUIF as working infrastructure — cited by work on speculative parallelism for multiprocessors and by the OlyMPIx parallelization tool as the compiler they start from — and as an entry in surveys of the field, from the ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems account of data and memory optimization for embedded systems to reviews of parallelization tools. Both roles attach to the SUIF project as a whole rather than to this paper's particular argument.
bruening:fddo:2000: Softspec's citation record is largely unjudged, and the judged portion is small, so only modest claims are possible. What that portion shows is a place in the thread-level speculation literature: the TOPLAS survey of compiler-driven software speculation covers it, work on a speculative mechanism for barrier synchronization adopts its idea, and studies of thread-level speculation for web applications and JavaScript engines cite it when motivating speculation without hardware support, while master/slave speculative parallelization positions itself against it. When the paper is cited substantively, it is as a demonstration that speculative parallelism needs no special hardware.
thies:mm:2009: External reception of the technique is thin. The works that cite it are mostly surveys and adjacent literature: a survey of compression-domain image and video processing places it as the lossless entry in its map of the area, the Foundations and Trends treatment of pattern matching in compressed texts and images notes it, and Kremlin gives it one of the record's few detailed readings. The idea of computing directly on LZ77-compressed data traveled mainly along the path the summary describes — into the compiler unifying lossless compression with sparse computing — rather than through independent adopters.
kjolstad:oopsla:2017:
Beyond the project, the citing literature divides into a broad periphery and a working core. The periphery names taco in a sentence as the compiler approach to sparse tensor algebra; the core builds on it. DISTAL and SpDISTAL extend the compiler to distributed tensor algebra, Mosaic extends it to interoperate with external kernels, and SparseLNR and the compilation of modular and general sparse workspaces carry its code generation further. Other systems use it as infrastructure: BaCO autotunes against it, and architecture-side work such as The Sparse Abstract Machine and Phloem builds hardware compilation paths with it.

The compiler also serves as the field's measuring stick. Accelerator papers beginning with ExTensor take its generated kernels as the software baseline, formal work such as Indexed Streams takes its fused loops as the object to reason about, and dozens of evaluations reuse its workloads or position new sparse compilers relative to it. Taken together, the record shows a system run and extended by a core of follow-on projects, surrounded by a large literature for which taco is the default point of reference in sparse tensor compilation.
solar-lezama:pldi:2005: In the wider literature the paper stands as the origin of sketching, and most substantive citations engage the idea rather than the StreamBit implementation. The generalization came quickly: Combinatorial sketching for finite programs carried the approach beyond bit-streaming and became the main reference for the Sketch line. The idea was adopted elsewhere — for synthesizing probabilistic programs, for synthesizing machine code from semantics, and for automated feedback generation for introductory programming assignments — while SMT-based optimization of embedded arithmetic measured against it. The larger mass of citations is list membership, crediting the paper in a sentence as the point where sketch-based synthesis began.
maydan:popl:1993: Among external citers the paper serves mostly as a reference point: array data-flow and privatization work positions itself against its precision-versus-cost tradeoff, and empirical papers cite its results as evidence that element-wise analysis pays off in parallelization. Direct construction on it is rarer but concrete — SUIF Explorer incorporates the analysis, a later line improves and reimplements the accurate array data-flow analysis, and communication-optimization work for parallelizing compilers adopts its exposed-set machinery to eliminate redundant messages. Much of the remaining record is passing mention in surveys of compiler transformations, and a sizable fraction of the external citations is unjudged.
thies:dna:2006: Reception came chiefly from the design-automation community for microfluidic biochips. There the paper's mixing algorithm, rather than its layered architecture, is the working object: a line of sample-preparation papers — on layout-aware, efficient, robust, and multi-target mixture preparation and dilution — takes it as the baseline method to improve upon, while others build dilution algorithms on its ideas or use it inside larger flows such as assay locking against bio-IP theft. The abstraction-layer argument itself surfaces mainly in passing mentions and survey citations, so in the citing literature the paper functions less as a programming-systems proposal than as the reference dilution algorithm.
karczmarek:lctes:2003: Outside the group the citation record is modest and stays close to stream compilation. The most engaged use is in mobile sensing, where work on static memory management builds on the schedules and a follow-on line adopts the ideas; scheduling papers such as the buffer-space efficient, deadlock-free work of Park and Dally cite its results as evidence about the code-size and buffer-space tradeoff. Evaluations of other stream systems reuse its benchmarks, and most remaining citations are brief mentions situating new schedulers against StreamIt. It is a paper cited within one community — mostly as background, occasionally as a foundation.
hall:lcpc:1995: External engagement clusters around the SUIF system itself: the studies measuring and evaluating automatic parallelization in SUIF run the framework, SUIF Explorer builds interactive parallelization on top of it, and the case for combining compile-time and run-time parallelization extends the analyses. Farther out, the paper appears in surveys and reference works on parallel computing and in passing citations crediting interprocedural analysis as an ingredient of automatic parallelization. The record is small, and close to half of the external citations are unjudged, so the visible reception is chiefly the SUIF community building on its own foundation.
ariya:cc:2002: Externally, the deepest engagement builds with the compiler itself. A line of secure-computation systems — Shechi, Decor, and a secure multiple-imputation pipeline — implements on top of Codon, and Vectron uses it as the substrate for auto-vectorizing dynamic programming; interpreter-testing work and an empirical study of the performance and energy of compiled Python treat it as a system under test. The rest of the record is thinner: Python-compilation papers such as HiPy reuse its benchmarks or compare against it, and list mentions place it among approaches to accelerating Python. The citation record is small, but its substantive uses are genuine system-building.
chan:sc:2009: The external record is small and mostly illustrative. Surveys of machine learning in compiler optimization and of automated multigrid-solver development cite the work as an example of autotuning over algorithmic choice with accuracy as a tunable parameter, and floating-point precision-tuning work credits the same idea. Within multigrid itself, papers on optimizing geometric multigrid for multicore and manycore processors and on communication-avoiding operators position their approaches against it rather than build on it. Direct extension of the method came from within the project, so the external reception is citation-as-example rather than adoption — a paper known for its idea more than its artifact.
del2017common: Beyond that follow-on, the external record is slender and mostly taxonomic. Surveys of FPGA programming abstractions and of high-level synthesis tools and toolchains place FROST among DSL-to-FPGA backends, and papers such as iPIM and work on transformations of high-level synthesis codes cite it as one instance of the DSL-to-HLS route. A few applied efforts in hardware-accelerated image and signal processing cite its speedups as evidence that FPGA acceleration pays. There is little building on the system outside its authors' orbit; in the literature the paper stands as a catalogued point in the design space of FPGA toolchains.
askit-cgo24: The citation record is thin and almost entirely peripheral. Works on prompt programming and LLM-driven code generation — APPL and DSL-Xpert among them — cite AskIt in passing as one of the languages for integrating LLM calls into programs, and a survey of interaction techniques in generative AI applications lists it alongside other interfaces. The remaining mentions come from applied LLM papers on subjects from malware deobfuscation to financial forecasting, citing it briefly for context. None of the judged citations engages the DSL's mechanisms in depth; the reception is list membership in a broad literature on programming with language models.
kotkar:hci4cid:2008: Its citation record is slight and consists of passing mentions. The citing works come from the literature on voice interfaces for development — the spoken web application framework, spoken query systems for agricultural commodity prices, community-driven maps for developing regions, and studies of interactive voice response as a participatory medium — each naming the Audio Wiki in a sentence among prior voice-based systems for low-literacy users. Most of the external citations are unjudged, and none of the judged ones engages the design, so the paper survives in that literature as one entry in the roll call of early spoken-web proposals.
thies:prib:2006: The workshop version itself drew only a handful of citations, all peripheral. Later work on protein structure prediction — support-vector-machine applications and neural-network fold recognition among them — cites it when reviewing prior secondary-structure methods, sometimes describing the HM-SVM approach in a paragraph but never building on it directly. The thin record is consistent with the expanded journal article serving as the main point of entry to the work, leaving the workshop paper a minor trace in the citation graph.
perkins:sosp:2009:
The reception runs through the automatic program repair literature that formed in the years after publication. GenProg took up the idea of automatically generating and validating patches, and Le Goues and colleagues' systematic study of automated repair measured its methods against ClearView's results; a steady stream of later repair papers position their techniques relative to it, and surveys of the field include it as a demonstration that deployed binaries can be patched without source code or human intervention.

Direct extensions are fewer but concrete: Schulte, DiLorenzo, and Weimer extended automated repair to binary and assembly programs on embedded devices, and Azim, Neamtiu, and Marvel carried automated patching to smartphone software. Beyond this engaged center, the bulk of the citing record is peripheral — ClearView appears in lists of repair and self-healing systems, or as evidence that runtime patching of deployed software is feasible — the pattern of a paper cited less for its machinery than for the possibility it demonstrated.
ragankelley:halide:2012: In the citing record the paper serves as the gateway to the language itself: much of its reception comes from work that programs in Halide rather than merely discussing it. Camera pipelines including burst photography for high dynamic range imaging on mobile cameras and Fast Fourier Color Constancy were written in the language; Mullapudi and colleagues automated Halide scheduling; later work made Halide pipelines differentiable, translated existing image processing libraries into Halide, and retargeted the compiler to heterogeneous hardware and FPGAs through systems such as HeteroHalide. Around these users sits a broad periphery that cites the paper as the representative image-processing DSL when framing new compilers and languages.
thies:ecoop:2005: The citing literature treats the paper mainly as a reference point: most citations are passing mentions in the related work of race and deadlock detectors, and surveys of testing for concurrent software list it among the static approaches. The engaged minority comes from successors in static deadlock detection — Naik, Park, and Sen position their detector against the lock-order-graph analysis — and one study reused its library subjects to compare the cost-effectiveness of static analysis and model checking for finding deadlocks. Few works build on the analysis itself; the paper settled into related-work sections as the treatment of deadlock freedom at the library interface.
zhao:vee:2011: The reception centers on the false sharing detectors that followed. SHERIFF, PREDATOR, and Cheetah position their designs against its instrumentation-based approach, ScaAnalyzer differentiates its scalability analysis from it, and the DARWIN framework adopted its ideas for detecting false sharing in OpenMP applications. A second strand cites the paper as evidence — that false sharing degrades performance on multicore machines, or that dynamic binary instrumentation can expose it — while the remaining citations are passing mentions in work on contention, scheduling, and performance analysis. The engaged readership is small and concentrated among builders of sharing detectors, for whom the tool is the design each successor explains itself against.
thies:pldi:2001: Within the polyhedral compilation literature the framework became part of the standard background: works on automatic parallelization, AlphaZ, and the Sparse Polyhedral Framework cite it in passing when surveying affine scheduling and memory optimization. The engaged reception is narrower and mathematical. Darte and Schreiber's lattice-based memory allocation examines the occupancy-vector formulation in detail, and Touati and Eisenbeis carried the joint schedule–storage view into periodic register allocation on ILP processors, with later work adopting the formulation for periodic task scheduling with storage minimization; a study of LLM-guided loop optimization returned to its examples as benchmarks. The citations are not numerous, but those that engage do so with the mathematics.
kjolstad:tog:2016: Outside the project, citing works engage Simit chiefly as a design point in the space of domain-specific languages. Tensor Comprehensions and Taichi position their abstractions against Simit's dual graph-and-matrix view, SymX measures its symbolic-expression simulator against Simit as a baseline, and papers across graphics and compiler venues list it as an example of a language built for physical simulation. Much of the remainder is passing mention in work on simulation and sparse linear algebra, so the deep external engagement is thin: Simit appears more often as the system others define themselves relative to than as one they extend.
bhive: The suite found the use it was built for: the citing literature consists largely of work that runs on BHive rather than work that merely mentions it. Abel and Reineke validate their throughput predictors and the uiCA simulator on it, DiffTune tunes CPU-simulator parameters against its measurements, COMET uses it to explain neural cost models, and several studies of transformer models over low-level programs draw their basic blocks from it; a microbenchmarking toolkit adopts its measurement methodology. The community is small and concentrated in basic-block performance modeling, but within that community BHive serves as common ground for validation.
barua:toc:2001: The citing record is modest and settles mainly in embedded-systems compilation, where software-managed memory outlived Raw. Barua's subsequent work on scratch-pad memory allocation engages the bank-disambiguation techniques in detail, Cho, Paek, and Whalley position their memory-bank assignment methods for digital signal processors against it, and a survey of compiling for reconfigurable computing places it among approaches to software-exposed memory. The rest of the citations are passing mentions, several from the pointer-analysis literature. Few works extend the techniques themselves; the article is cited for what it showed — that a compiler can place data well when memory banks are visible to software.
del2018: External reception is slight and mostly taxonomic. Surveys of FPGA programming and of high-level synthesis toolchains include FROST among the systems that carry DSLs to hardware, the stateful dataflow multigraphs work positions its data-centric approach relative to FROST's scheduling co-language, and high-level synthesis compilers such as AnyHLS and FLOWER cite it among prior DSL-to-hardware efforts. Few external works build on the system itself; its main uptake ran through Tiramisu, and elsewhere it stands as one entry in the catalogue of paths from high-level languages to FPGAs.
chen:graphics-hardware:2005: A small citation record splits between two communities. In graphics architecture, a power-aware reconfigurable rendering engine adopted the idea of reallocating pipeline resources, work on dynamic reconfigurable shaders for embedded graphics positions itself against the compile-time approach, and GRAMPS and later work on fine-grain scheduling of pipeline parallelism cite the paper as an example of mapping the graphics pipeline onto programmable parallel hardware. In the streaming community, its rendering workloads reappear as benchmarks for mapping stream programs to multicore processors. Most mentions are brief, and the paper reads in the literature as a data point on reconfigurable rendering rather than a foundation later systems built on.
taco-lossless-cgo22: External reception beyond that lineage is thin, and most of it is passing: papers on compressed set representations, grammar-compressed matrix multiplication, entropy decoding for sparse kernels on GPUs, and kernel generation for quantized language models mention the paper when noting that computation can proceed without decompression. The one detailed external engagement, on optimizing compression schemes for parallel sparse tensor algebra, works through the technique itself, and later work on sparse and structured tensor compilers cites its results in support. The idea's clearest continuation runs inside its own line rather than through the external record.
wilson:sigplan:1994:
The same relationship extended well beyond the group. In the judged external record the dominant citation act is use: the citing papers report research carried out inside SUIF, and an unusual share of them are core engagements rather than passing mentions. Wilson and Lam's context-sensitive pointer analysis for C was built in the infrastructure, as were Ghosh, Martonosi, and Malik's cache miss equations and their extension to caches of arbitrary associativity, Rivera and Tseng's data transformations for eliminating conflict misses, Beyls and D'Hollander's reuse-distance work, and Tseng's elimination of barrier synchronization.

The platform also crossed subfields. SUIF Explorer built directly on it; Liao, Devadas, and Keutzer used it for storage assignment to decrease code size; PICO-NPA used it in high-level synthesis of nonprogrammable hardware accelerators; the Zephyr abstract-syntax work took it as a subject of study. A thinner band of citations simply names SUIF as the example of a shared research compiler. On the whole the paper is cited less for its claims than for the system it distributes — reception in the form of work done with the tool.
taylor:isca:2004: Beyond the project the evaluation is read in two registers. A band of core citations comes from groups that used the chip as an experimental substrate: thermal modeling and management of on-chip networks, gigabit routing on the software-exposed tiled microprocessor, a reconfigurable architecture for load-balanced rendering, software-based instruction caching for embedded processors, and the conservation cores work. A larger mass cites the measurements as evidence, drawing on the Pentium-III comparisons and stream results in arguments about tiled architectures. Most citations, though, are peripheral, placing Raw in lists of tiled and multicore designs, and a small part of the influence is routed through successor tiled processors rather than the paper itself.
ansel:cgo:2011: External reception came mostly from the approximate-computing literature, which absorbed it as an example. Mittal's survey of approximate computing places it among language-level approaches, a Proceedings of the IEEE retrospective does the same, and the Wang and O'Boyle survey of machine learning in compiler optimization lists its evolutionary search. Systems papers such as Paraprox position their own approximation schemes against its compile-time autotuning, and a smaller band reuses its benchmarks, the canary-input work on dynamically steered approximation among them. Nearly all of these citations are peripheral: the paper is a fixture of related-work sections on trading accuracy for performance, and only EMEURO, an accelerator-generation framework, built on the system directly.
thies:micro:2007: In the citing literature the paper travels mostly as a passing reference: much of its record is unjudged, and among the judged citations the majority name it in a sentence in related-work discussions of pipeline parallelism, often in architecture papers some distance from its topic. A small engaged band did more. Komoda, Miwa, and Nakamura adopted the communication-overlap idea for OpenCL applications, JFlow reused its case studies to evaluate refactorings for flow-based parallelism, Fussli measured against it as a baseline, and a cache-based scheme for speculative parallelization adopted one of its ideas. The reception is that of a practical technique noted often and taken up occasionally.
larsen:pact:2002: External reception settled in the short-vector compilation community, for which alignment was a shared obstacle. Eichenberger, Wu, and O'Brien's vectorization for SIMD architectures with alignment constraints engages the paper in detail, the CELL processor compiler cites it as evidence, and work on runtime alignment and length conversion, on multi-platform auto-vectorization, and on SIMD compilation for embedded processors positions its own alignment handling relative to it. The idea traveled outside compilers as well: T4 adopted the congruence idea in compiling sequential code for speculative parallelization in hardware. The citations are not numerous and many are brief, but the detailed engagements come from groups whose own work centered on alignment analysis.
tyler:ppopp:2016: Subsequent citing work keeps it in that role of reference point. Stencil papers measure against it — a roofline-guided multi-stencil CFD solver and instruction-stream scheduling work for stencils on ARM processors take it as the distributed baseline — while distributed machine-learning systems, among them work on dataflow-graph partitioning for very large models and on breaking the computation-communication abstraction barrier, position their handling of communication relative to its schedule-level approach. One effort built on the system itself, extending it to distributed and heterogeneous SAR backprojection with Halide. The record is small but a good share of it is substantive: the paper serves as the point of comparison for expressing distribution in the schedule.
bruening:cgo:2005: External reception likewise comes from builders. The dynamic binary translation community treats the paper as a reference on code-cache consistency and capacity: the DynamoRIO line extended it to thread-shared and to process-shared, persistent code caches, while independent systems engage it on its own ground — fragment-cache management for embedded scratchpads and work on reducing pressure in bounded DBT code caches position their schemes against it, and HDTrans, generators of low-overhead binary translators, and the process-level redundancy work on transient fault tolerance cite its measurements as evidence. The remaining citations are brief mentions in the same literature; almost nothing cites the paper from outside the community that manages code caches.
larsen:micro:2005: Citations from elsewhere are few and mostly brief: the paper appears in related-work lists on SIMD code generation — dynamic-programming selection of vector instructions, Liquid SIMD, data-layout transformation for stencils — typically in a sentence noting that vectorization can be applied selectively. A handful go further. Hampton and Asanović built on the compiler in implementing virtual memory in a vector processor with software restart markers, a dissertation on SIMD-aware word-length optimization adopted its approach, and work mapping streaming languages to general-purpose processors through vectorization discusses the algorithm in detail. The reception is confined to the short-vector compilation community, and modest even there.
pacula:evoapps:2012: The record beyond the project is thin and almost entirely peripheral, and part of its influence runs through the SiblingRivalry autotuner it served rather than the paper itself. Surveys carry most of what there is: Wang and O'Boyle's surveys of machine learning in compiler optimization list the study among autotuning applications, and a survey of adaptive operator selection for meta-heuristics places it in that lineage. Online-learning papers on bandits and perturbation techniques cite it as an applied example, Tensor Comprehensions names it in passing among autotuning precedents, and HybridTuner discusses the hyperparameter question in some detail. Cited by surveyors more than builders, the reception matches its role as a focused companion study.
chou:2022:dynamic-formats: Its citations are few and sit at the edges of their papers, coming from the sparse-compilation community the TACO line addresses. The structured-tensor-algebra work of Ghorbani, Bauer, and Grosser engages it most directly, discussing the node-schema approach while compressing structured tensors; WingSpan, Bonsai, and work on optimizing sparse tensor compilation for sparse output cite it as an instance of what format-general compilers cover; a paper on exploiting sparsity in convolutional networks on GPUs cites a finding as evidence. None of the judged citations builds on the system itself, so the paper functions as a boundary marker — cited to note that mutable, pointer-based sparse structures are within a compiler's reach.
bernstein-kjolstad:2016: As a position piece it is cited for its argument, though most of its citation record is unjudged and the judged portion is a handful. That handful comes from the community the argument addressed: the Taichi line of simulation languages invokes it when motivating compiler support for simulation — QuanTaichi and MeshTaichi both cite it — and IMESH, a DSL for mesh processing in the same journal, takes up the argument directly. A study of generating sounds for soft bodies and a SIGGRAPH Talks piece on the look and lighting of Frozen 2 show it reaching practitioners. The article is cited to justify building new simulation languages — the outcome it argued for.
larsen:pldi:2000:
Beyond the group's own successors, the citing literature made superword-level parallelism a research area in its own right. One line reworks the packing algorithm itself: PSLP, VW-SLP, and SuperGraph-SLP restructure how statements are grouped and searched, while the SIMD defragmenter and a compiler framework for extracting superword level parallelism measure their techniques against the original scheme. Another line, running through Superword-Level Parallelism in the Presence of Control Flow and Exploiting Superword-Level Locality in Multimedia Extension Architectures, carried the approach to branching code and to the memory hierarchy, and the compiler found an early user in the DIVA processing-in-memory chip project.

Around that core sits a much larger body of citation that treats SLP as shared vocabulary: papers on automatic vectorization position their techniques against it, cite its measurements as evidence for the value of parallelism inside basic blocks, or list it among the standard approaches alongside loop vectorization. Most of these engagements are brief, but the substantive minority — the works extending, adopting, or benchmarking against the algorithm — is large enough to form a distinct SLP vectorization literature, with this paper at its root.
stephenson:cgo:2005: In the wider literature the paper functions mostly as an early exhibit of machine learning applied inside a compiler: the bulk of its citations are brief mentions in surveys and related-work discussions of learned compilation, citing it as an early demonstration rather than engaging its classifiers. A smaller group adopts the method as a template, training supervised models to predict other decisions — heterogeneous task partitioning, thread-coarsening on graphics processors, transactional-memory tuning, loop iteration counts, and unroll factors in high-level synthesis — while work on automatic feature generation and on selecting optimizations from performance counters measures itself against it. Direct extensions are rare; the paper's reach is as a precedent and a recipe.
bruening:vee:2012: Reception follows the tool rather than the analysis: the most substantive citations come from systems built on DynamoRIO — fuzzers such as ICS3Fuzzer and Terminator, the Taint Rabbit's taint tracking, and reverse-engineering tools including RePEconstruct, dynStruct, and DYBS — which cite the paper as the account of the platform they run on, often in security settings where transparency against uncooperative code matters. A second group cites its transparency requirements as evidence when discussing what dynamic binary instrumentation can and cannot hide, and Engineering Record and Replay for Deployability takes the system as a point of comparison for its own design. Much of the rest is list membership among instrumentation frameworks.
barua:isca:1999: External reception is modest and stays close to the architecture.
