In the tiled-processor and reconfigurable-computing literature Maps appears as the worked example of a memory system managed entirely by the compiler — Hartenstein's retrospective on reconfigurable computing lists it in that role, and work on coarse-grain pipelining across FPGA architectures borrows the idea of compiler-orchestrated data placement. The deeper engagements are few: Taylor's account of tiled microprocessors builds on the system, and modulo unrolling reappears in affine loop optimization for Chapel. Most other citations are brief, and the paper's imprint is best read through the Raw project it served rather than through independent adoption.
amarasinghe:lcpc:1993: Citations to the overview read it as the citable description of the SUIF parallelizing compiler rather than as a technique paper. Works built on the same infrastructure point to it when describing their setting — linear scan register allocation and Rugina and Rinard's symbolic bounds analysis and recursion unrolling among them — and embedded-systems research on application scenarios cites the compiler as machinery. Elsewhere the paper appears in lists of parallelizing compilers alongside the polytope-model literature. Engagement with the three-phase design itself is rare, and much of the citing record is brief, so the reception is best described as acknowledgment of the infrastructure the overview documents.
zhao:cgo:2008: What the citing literature took up is PiPA's central idea — decoupling analysis from execution and running it as a parallel pipeline — more than the prototype itself. TaintPipe carries pipelined processing into symbolic taint analysis, ShadowReplica positions its own decoupled taint tracking relative to PiPA, and work on dynamic binary parallelization and on data-flow tracking systems adopts the compact-profile approach. A concurrent dynamic analysis framework for multicore hardware measures itself against PiPA directly. The remaining citations are mostly brief, placing the system in lists of attempts to hide instrumentation cost with spare cores.
og-cgo20: Among external citers the paper serves mainly as a point of comparison: the evaluation of graph frameworks on the GAP Benchmark Suite, work on efficient stepping algorithms for parallel shortest paths, and a scalable architecture for reprioritizing ordered parallelism all measure against the ordered GraphIt implementations, and Cache-Efficient Fork-Processing Patterns on Large Graphs draws on its findings. The larger remainder is list membership, with hardware accelerators and concurrent graph systems such as GraphPulse and Glign citing it among the compilers and frameworks for ordered graph processing. The engaged citations are comparative rather than constructive — outside the group's own successors, the paper is measured against more often than built on.
g2-cgo21: The external record is compact and split between comparison and cataloguing. Work on decoupling schedule, topology layout, and algorithm in GPU graph processing takes G2 as a baseline, an FPGA high-level-synthesis study of graph analysis measures against it, and Voyager builds on it for graph neural networks; a survey of optimization techniques for GPU programming in ACM Computing Surveys covers its scheduling space. Most other citations list G2 among GPU graph frameworks — A Programming Model for GPU Load Balancing and several accelerator papers cite it in that role — a modest but substantive early reception for a system whose ideas also travel through its successors.
randomwalk-iiswc21: The citing literature is small but concrete. The open-source implementations found users: work on sparsifying graph neural networks, including a compressive-sensing variant, builds on them, and Towards Real-Time Temporal Graph Learning measures against the paper's characterization. GENTI, a GPU system for walk-based subgraph extraction, positions itself relative to the study, and Mint's accelerator for temporal motif mining cites its findings on workload behavior. The remaining citations are passing mentions in papers on graph accelerators and temporal graph learning, where the characterization appears as background rather than as a result in use.
revec-cc: The record of citations is thin, and much of it is brief. What gets reused is the benchmark suite: the study of vector processing for mobile devices and work combining run-time checks with compile-time analysis for control-flow auto-vectorization both draw on Revec's intrinsic-rich kernels. Elsewhere Revec appears as an example in work on moving vectorized code across instruction sets — the Lasagne static binary translator and a survey of MIMD execution on SIMD machines cite it in that role — and a journal article on code rejuvenation from vector intrinsics to portable standardized SIMD carries the rejuvenation framing forward. No external system extends the pass itself.
bosboom:oopsla:2014: External take-up of the commensal approach is limited. LaminarIR, with its compile-time queues for structured streams, measures its performance against StreamJIT, and that is the one sustained engagement in the record. The other citations are list placements: RaftLib and Streams a la carte name StreamJIT among stream programming systems, and an application of OpenTuner to GPU compiler parameters lists it among systems that delegate tuning decisions to OpenTuner. The record is small enough that reception reads as recognition among stream-language designers rather than adoption of commensal compilation elsewhere.
ansel:pldi:2009:
Beyond the project, the reception is broad but mostly at arm's length: to the citing literature PetaBricks is the name for algorithmic choice, and the bulk of the record cites it as the representative of that idea, in related-work lists, in surveys of autotuning and adaptive software, and as the design point against which new systems are positioned. A smaller band engaged directly. Elastic computing adopted the multiple-implementation premise, variant-based competitive parallel execution raced alternative variants of sequential programs, and HPAC drew on the approach for approximate computing in HPC OpenMP applications; a handful of works ran the compiler and autotuner themselves, among them parallel iterative compilation and a student reimplementation of PetaBricks in Julia.

The pattern is that of a reference point rather than a substrate: few external systems build on the implementation, but the vocabulary the paper introduced, poly-algorithms assembled from alternative rules and tuned alongside parameters, recurs wherever an autotuner's search space includes the algorithm itself, and part of the influence traveled onward through the project's own successors, OpenTuner among them.
amarasinghe:pldi:1993: In the citing literature the paper serves chiefly as a fixed point of the distributed-memory compilation era: work on message-passing code generation positions its methods against the value-centric, polyhedral formulation, and much of the remaining record is brief. The sustained line of building is Ferner's, whose Paraguin compiler generated message-passing code using SUIF, whose later work revisited communication code generation algorithms for message-passing systems, and whose work on suppressing independent loops in packing nests extends the machinery directly. The decomposition literature, from Anderson's automatic computation and data decomposition to the Rice dHPF overpartitioning work and the EPPP compiler, took up its representations, and DISTAL carries the same concerns into distributed tensor algebra.
zhang:bigdata:2017: The citing literature took up the paper in two roles. Its diagnosis, that fast graph frameworks stall on memory for most of their cycles, is cited as motivating evidence across graph-processing research, and its results serve as a measuring stick: the I-GCN accelerator, hardware-assisted propagation blocking, and learning-based data reordering all compare against CSR segmenting. The technique itself traveled as well. VGL adapted segmenting to the NEC SX-Aurora TSUBASA vector architecture, GNNIE to GNN inference, and GPU systems such as HyTGraph build on the partitioning scheme, while work on practical parallel hypergraph algorithms reuses the framework directly. A good share of the citations does something with the idea rather than merely naming it.
sermulins:lctes:2005: Reception concentrates in the stream-programming community the work grew from. The catalog of stream processing optimizations in ACM Computing Surveys records the transformations with this paper among its sources, and detailed discussions outnumber extensions: Moonen's work on predictable embedded multiprocessor architectures carried the cache-aware view to streaming applications on multiprocessor systems-on-chip, later work on generalized cache tiling for dataflow programs measures against the fusion strategy, and stream-processing optimizations for mobile sensing use it as a point of comparison. Others reuse the StreamIt benchmarks the evaluation established, software-pipelined execution of stream programs on GPUs among them. The record is modest in size but grounded: most citations come from people working on the same problem.
sullivan:ivme:2003: Outside the project the technique found few direct users, LIFT applying the same instrumentation substrate to information-flow tracking for security, and the record is otherwise mostly peripheral: the paper appears in passing wherever interpreter overhead or trace formation is discussed, and the survey of adaptive optimization in virtual machines fixes its place among the era's approaches. The closer engagements come from the interpreter-implementation literature: context threading cites its findings, YETI positions its own design against it, and Tracing the meta-level gives it one of its more detailed readings. The approach stands in the literature as an early attempt to make trace-based optimization see through an interpreter to the program it runs.
ansel:cases:2012: The external citation record is thin in extensions and plain about it: no citing system adopts the racing design, and most references are brief mentions in the online-autotuning and adaptive-systems literature. Where the paper is discussed at length it is as a design point; Wang and O'Boyle's account of machine learning in compiler optimization describes the approach, and mARGOt situates its own dynamic autotuning framework relative to it. The most consistent audience is the self-aware and energy-aware systems line around Hoffmann, where JouleGuard, CoAdapt, and MEANTIME cite it among prior adaptive systems. In that literature SiblingRivalry figures as an example of always-on adaptation, cited for the idea more than built upon.
bruening:fddo:2001: Among the examined citations the reception is that of infrastructure: many come from work that ran the framework rather than merely mentioning it. Vigilante and the foreign-code detection work on the Windows/x86 platform built on it; Smith and Hazelwood's study of code cache management and later measurements of dynamic binary translators' hardware-cache impact took it as a subject system; work on indirect branch emulation in virtual machines drew on it as tooling. Duesterwald's account of the design and engineering of a dynamic binary optimizer revisits the same ground from the Dynamo side. Many citing works are unjudged, so the picture is partial, but among the judged, users outnumber mentioners, unusual for a workshop paper.
zhao:pact:2006: The record around it is small, and its center of gravity moved toward security analysis: TaintPipe adopted the idea of a compact recorded profile driving a later analysis for pipelined symbolic taint tracking, and StraightTaint extended it into decoupled offline taint analysis, putting the profile to uses the original paper did not anticipate. PiPA likewise built directly on the work. Elsewhere the engagement is documentary: tracing and debugging systems such as ONTRAC and work on hierarchical program paths discuss the profile's design, and PROMPT measures its own memory-profiling framework against it. The citations are few, but a good share come from people building comparable machinery.
vemal-neurips: Citing works engage Vemal almost entirely from a distance: none extends the method or deploys the learned policy, and the record is peripheral throughout. The paper is cited instead as an example, one of the demonstrations that learned policies can stand in for hand-written compiler heuristics, in the survey of machine learning for computer architecture and systems, in the taxonomy of ML for systems problems, and in the related-work sections of learned-optimization efforts such as ProGraML, RL4ReAl, and work on vectorization heuristics in dynamic compilers. The literature records it as a data point in a trend rather than a foundation.
mueller_sparse_2020: Reception is quiet and specific, confined to the sparse tensor systems community. ALTO and the work on compiling modular and general sparse workspaces cite its findings as supporting evidence, and one successor engages head-on: On Higher-performance Sparse Tensor Transposition positions its own algorithms directly against Quesadilla. The remaining references are brief mentions in work on sparsity-aware tensor decomposition, data layout for sparse tensor kernels on GPUs, and autoscheduling for sparse frameworks. The citations are few, as befits a brief announcement, but the closest reader is the one trying to transpose tensors faster.
shajii:oopsla:2019: The citing record is small but leans toward use: bioinformatics systems adopted Seq as working infrastructure, from segmental-duplication analysis of genome assemblies to the Sequre framework for secure multiparty computation over biomedical data and its successor Shechi. Some of that engagement reaches the language through the Codon compiler it grew into, and the remainder of the citations name Seq among high-performance languages for the domain rather than engaging its design.
olszewski:asplos:2009:
Beyond the project, deterministic multithreading grew into a research area, and the citing literature treats Kendo as one of its reference points. Most citations position new determinism systems against it or list it among the software-only approaches, but a core engaged closely: Dthreads measures itself against Kendo, RCDC builds on it, and work on deterministic multithreading without global barriers and on memory-isolated determinism (esDMT) takes up its scheduling ideas. Its deterministic logical time, built from hardware performance counters, is the element most often carried forward.

The idea also traveled outside the determinism literature. Bunshin applies it to compositing security mechanisms through diversification, Memoir draws on it for state continuity in protected modules, work on detecting covert timing channels adopts it for time-deterministic replay, and FiberSCIP carries it into parallel mathematical optimization; real-time work uses Kendo as a baseline for worst-case execution-time calculation on multicores. The long tail of the record is peripheral — Kendo named in a sentence about determinism — but the engaged citations span systems, security, debugging, and solvers.
stephenson:pldi:2000: The analysis found its main audience in hardware compilation. High-level synthesis took up bitwidth inference as a recurring concern: Cong's group built bitwidth-aware scheduling and binding on the idea, and later work on range and bitmask analysis for hardware optimization extends the technique directly. BitValue inference, developed independently at about the same time, is a companion work cited alongside it, and the wordlength-allocation line of Constantinides, Cheung, and Luk treats the paper as a point of comparison. The benchmarks traveled as well — bitwidth-aware global register allocation reuses them — and a long tail of citations invokes the reported area, clock, and power gains as evidence that narrow-width computation is worth exploiting.
thies:ictd:2009: In the wider literature the paper functions chiefly as evidence: mobile-health and ICTD studies cite its error rates when weighing forms, SMS, and voice against one another, and surveys — from the Cochrane review of self-administered survey methods to the account of user interface design for low-literate and novice users — fold it into their pictures of data collection in resource-poor settings. Closer engagement is rarer: Lerer's IVR rendering platform takes the study as its baseline, but few citing papers extend the method itself. Most citations are peripheral, which suits a measured comparison: many papers need the finding, few need more.
hall:toplas:2005: As the archival form of work whose earlier versions had already circulated, the article draws a modest citation record, most of it brief: papers cite it as the reference for SUIF's interprocedural parallelization or as evidence of what automatic parallelization achieved on scientific codes. The closest engagement comes from lines that continued the analyses — Hall's own work on predicated array data-flow analysis measures against it, her code isolator and empirical sparse-solver study draw on it, and Rus and Rauchwerger's work on migrating sequential code to multi-threaded architectures takes it as a baseline. Farther afield the citations thin to passing mentions in later parallelization work, from behavior-oriented parallelization to Futhark.
thies:ppopp:2005: Reception of the construct divides between the project's orbit and the dataflow community. Within StreamIt, teleport messaging is exercised by application studies — stream programming for image and video compression, image-based motion estimation — and a sizable share of the citing record is the project's own. Outside it, the closest engagement comes from Edward A. Lee's group: Bui, Patel, and Lee adopt the sdep formalism to check circular dependencies in distributed stream programs, and Bui's dissertation on scheduling stream programs extends it. Elsewhere the paper is described more than used — SoC-C differentiates its own treatment of control in embedded software, and many citations recount the mechanism in detail without building on it.
mendis:pldi:2015: Later work cites Helium mainly as a fixed point in the design space of lifting: papers on raising legacy code to higher-level forms — verified lifting of stencil computations, automatic translation of image-processing libraries to Halide, trace-based affine reconstruction of codes — differentiate themselves from its dynamic, trace-driven approach, and Collie and O'Boyle's gray-box program lifting measures against it. As many citations name it as proof that stripped, optimized binaries can be lifted at all, motivating work from matching legacy code to heterogeneous APIs to hardware FFT accelerators. Direct reuse is rare — a temporal-blocking stencil study builds on it — so the paper stands as a demonstrated endpoint rather than a platform.
lamb:pldi:2003: External reception is quieter than the project's internal use: a sizable share of the citing record is StreamIt's own papers and theses, and most outside citations name the work in passing when listing the compiler's optimizations. The clearest line of uptake runs through sketching — Solar-Lezama's StreamBit takes the linear framework as its point of departure, and programming by sketching for bit-streaming programs carries that agenda forward — while the static-analysis community, in Feret's analysis of digital filters and Monniaux's compositional analysis of floating-point linear filters, cites it when treating linear filters as objects of formal study; Sigma* sets its own approach apart from this compile-time analysis.
agrawal:cases:2005: Outside the project the record is thin and mostly brief: stream-architecture and stream-compiler papers — software-pipelined execution on GPUs, Liquid Metal, the Fei Teng 64 stream processing system — name the analysis among StreamIt's optimizations rather than build on it. The more substantive engagements treat it as a neighbor to be distinguished from: Sigma* positions its own work against this compile-time framework, and the paper on fusing effectful comprehensions describes the approach closely. A record of this size and shape says the framework was noted more than adopted — its generality acknowledged, its machinery left to the project that built it.
anderson:ppopp:1995: The judged portion of the citation record concentrates in the locality-optimization literature: the sustained line of work by Kandemir, Ramanujam, and Choudhary on integrating loop and data transformations defines its frameworks against this paper's, returning to it in a compiler algorithm for optimizing locality in loop nests, matrix-based approaches to global locality, and an interprocedural framework. Work on tuning compiler optimizations for simultaneous multithreading positions itself the same way, and the remaining citations are brief mentions in later data-layout work. Most of the external record has not been judged, so the picture is partial; what it shows is a paper that combined loop-and-data frameworks named as their point of departure.
tseng:ics:1995: The citation record is small, and its judged portion is concentrated: the Kandemir–Ramanujam–Choudhary line on locality optimization cites the paper's findings as supporting evidence — that analyses a distributed-memory compiler must perform pay off as optimizations on shared-memory machines — and Tseng's own later work carries the argument forward. The rest are scattered passing mentions, in HPF benchmark compilation and software-cache management among them. Modest as it is, the record fits the paper's character: a position piece whose measurements are cited as evidence rather than a system to be built on.
agarwal:suif:1997: A problem statement rather than a solution, the workshop paper draws a small citing record, much of it unjudged. The engagement that exists is close to home: MIT theses building Raw's software stack — software-based instruction caching, software floating-point computation, the fabric hardware implementation — cite it as a working document of the compiler effort. Farther out, surveys of coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures and of reconfigurable computing systems include it in their accounts of the area. Its reception is that of a project charter, cited chiefly from within the project it chartered.
kiriansky-micro18-dawg:
In the citing literature DAWG stands as a fixed point in the design space of cache defenses. Much of the record is positional: papers proposing mitigations for speculative-execution and cache side-channel attacks place DAWG among the partitioning defenses and differentiate their designs from it, often by offering finer-grained or more scalable partitioning. Bespoke Cache Enclaves and Chunked-Cache measure against it as a baseline, as do speculation-focused defenses such as SpecShield and Speculative Privacy Tracking, and surveys of microarchitectural security put it in the partitioning branch of their taxonomies.

A smaller thread engages the security argument rather than the mechanism. Formal-methods work on modelling and verifying security-oriented resource partitioning takes DAWG as a subject, RTL2μPATH carries related questions into hardware security verification, attack-side works such as MicroScope and Safecracker pick up its ideas, and IVcache builds its evaluation directly against it. The great majority of citations, though, are brief: DAWG is a defense a paper in this area is expected to name, and most do so in a sentence or a table row.
lee:asplos:1998: The compiler carried much of the paper's reception: energy and power studies of tiled architectures and on-chip networks — the ISLPED energy characterization of a tiled processor, software-directed power-aware interconnection networks, high-level power analysis for on-chip networks — ran RAWCC in their experimental flows, and Swenson extended the spatial instruction scheduling directly. Within the project, Barua's compiler-managed memory line and Babb's compilation for gate-reconfigurable architectures grew out of the same machinery. Most other citations are briefer, naming the paper when introducing spatial compilation for distributed-resource machines, and part of its influence travels under the names of the later Raw papers rather than under its own.
urbanski:loc:2006: Beyond that line, the chip found users of its own: the device and its multiphase approach supported fluorescent molecular-logic-gate experiments, and Urbanski and colleagues carried it into metabolic profiling of single preimplantation embryos, while design-automation work on continuous-flow biochips later reused the architecture as a benchmark. Most of the citation record, though, sits in the field's broader literature — Micro Total Analysis Systems reviews and articles on microfluidic large-scale integration cite the paper as one entry in the catalogue of droplet-control techniques. The reception is that of a hardware paper absorbed into its field: a handful of direct uses, and a long tail of passing mention.
kjolstad:2018:workspaces: Among the paper's citers the sparse-compilation community predominates, and its engagement is unusually direct: a large fraction of the citing works extend or build on the transformation rather than merely mention it. MLIR's sparse tensor support adopts the workspace idea, and a line of TACO-descended systems — Mosaic, SparseLNR, and compilers for sparse tensor convolutions and shape operators — extends the mechanism itself, with later work on modular and general sparse workspaces generalizing the dense scratch arrays to sparse ones. Hardware-oriented compilers such as the Sparse Abstract Machine, Stardust, CoNST, and FuseFlow build on the generated kernels and the scheduling vocabulary. The record is small but dense with successors.
VarStudy2023: In the lattice-QCD literature the study's reception centers on its cautionary result. Papers on multi-baryon spectroscopy cite the interpolating-operator dependence as a systematic concern in interpreting two-nucleon spectra, and a follow-up by Detmold and collaborators extends the analysis with further constraints on the finite-volume spectrum at the same pion mass. The computed spectra serve as input elsewhere: a constraint of pionless effective field theory uses them directly, and calculations of neutrinoless double-beta decay in finite volume take them as benchmarks, while the sparsened-propagator machinery reappears in nucleon-pion spectroscopy. The other citations are brief mentions in the two-nucleon discussion and in reviews of the field.
drake:ipdps:2006: Elsewhere the decoder's afterlife is chiefly as a workload. The StreamIt MPEG-2 implementation joined the benchmark suites of compiler and architecture studies — a comparative evaluation of memory models for chip multiprocessors and Sigma*'s symbolic learning of stream filters both run it — and stream-language papers such as the Canals language cite the paper when arguing that video codecs suit the streaming model. Beyond these uses the citations are mostly list entries in discussions of stream-programming applications. The record is modest, but the program outlived its publication as a shared test case, which is what an application paper aims for.
amarasinghe:micro:1996: Citers treat the article less as an argument than as a handle for the SUIF parallelizer: most substantive citations come from work that uses the system. SUIF Explorer and compiler-directed page coloring build on the infrastructure within the Stanford orbit, a long line of embedded-systems and energy-optimization studies by Kandemir and colleagues cites the article for the compiler their experiments run on, and hardware/software co-compilation efforts from FPGA module mapping to the Nymble system do the same. The article's own thesis — that architects should design for parallelizing compilers — draws less direct engagement, surviving mainly in occasional passing references.
chen:pldi:2022: The citation record is mostly brief: auto-vectorization papers list the framework among SLP extensions when surveying the landscape, and systems such as Parsimony and DynVec cite it as an example of the genre. The engaged citations are positional — work on hybrid slice selection for SLP, on retrofitting control-flow graphs in LLVM IR for auto-vectorization, and the compiler-construction paper If-Convert as Early as You Must each set their designs against its predicate-based approach. The paper has entered the frame of reference for control-flow vectorization; whether Predicated SSA itself is taken up is a question the early record does not answer.
buildit-cgo21: External reception is thinner than the project's own lineage: outside the group, BuildIt appears mostly as an entry in the multi-stage-programming canon. Papers from that community — on partially evaluating symbolic interpreters, on multi-stage evaluators with let-insertion, and on mechanized semantics of staging annotations — cite it as the C++ point in the design space, and SABLE lists it among staging frameworks for sparse computation. eCC++ positions its embedded-DSL framework against it directly, while systems such as SLANG.D, Flan, and Exo 2 mention it in passing as related infrastructure. The citations are few but come from the community the paper addresses.
ansel:xrds:2010: The piece draws light citation of its own — the research credit flows to the PLDI paper — and its reception is correspondingly modest. Where it is cited, it serves as an accessible reference for PetaBricks and for autotuning in general: SPIRAL's account of extreme performance portability lists it among autotuning systems, papers on autotuning divide-and-conquer stencils and on autotuning exascale applications do the same, and work on programming and mapping strategies for runtime-adaptable embedded computing gives it a closer reading. The pattern suits the genre — an introduction written for students, cited when authors want an approachable entry to the idea.
arxiv:2005.04091: The preprint's citation trail is short. Of the citations it gathers, the most substantive comes from MLIR's sparse tensor compilation work, which names it as an example of a compiler treating sparsity in deep learning; the others — PIT's work on dynamic sparse models, a data-centric optimization framework for machine learning, a survey of trusted distributed AI — mention it in passing. The paper's role was demonstrative, and its influence is better read through the Tiramisu project it extended than through its own citation record.
ansel:ipdps:2009: The citation record bears that out: a large share of citing works run DMTCP rather than merely discuss it, and the tool turns up far from its original cluster targets — SweeD checkpoints likelihood computations over thousands of genomes, CRUM carries checkpoint-restart to CUDA's unified memory, and Kubernetes systems lean on it for stateful fault tolerance and seamless pod migration. The rest of the citations place DMTCP in the standard roster of transparent checkpointing packages.
bruening:cgo:2011: In the citing literature Dr. Memory serves chiefly as a yardstick. Memory-error detectors that followed — AddressSanitizer and MemorySanitizer among them — measure their speed and coverage against it, and the pattern repeats across use-after-free detection, uninitialized-read mitigation, firmware fuzzing, and shadow-memory monitoring. A second, larger body of citations simply places the tool in the standard roster of memory checkers, while binary-only fuzzing work puts the tool itself to use. Few papers build on its internals; its role in the literature is that of an established baseline against which new detectors are measured.
thies:nc:2007: External reception centers less on the abstraction layers than on the mixing algorithm beneath them. The digital-microfluidics literature on sample preparation treats the paper's dilution and mixing scheme as a point of departure: work on waste-aware dilution, reactant minimization with skewed mixing trees, and multi-target sample preparation measures new algorithms against it, while error-correcting and error-oblivious sample preparation on digital microfluidic biochips builds on it directly. Beyond that community the record consists mostly of brief mentions in the programmable-microfluidics literature; the layered-abstraction argument itself drew fewer direct successors than the algorithm it carried.
witchel:micro:2001: The citing literature engages the design chiefly in discussion rather than construction. Papers on way-halting caches, speculative way caching, and heterogeneous way-size caches describe the tag-unchecked access scheme in detail when setting out hardware-only routes to the same energy savings, and compiler-enabled approaches — Xtream-fit, and work coupling compiler-enabled with conventional memory accessing — measure against it. Most other citations are brief placements in the energy-efficient cache literature. The idea also resurfaces in another register: Ceviche adopts direct addressing in a capability-enhanced design for secure virtualization of caches.
lerer:dev:2010: The answer — not without training — is what the citing literature carries forward. Voice-interface work in ICTD and HCI cites the study chiefly as evidence about what untrained users can operate: 99DOTS and Learn2Earn draw on its findings, a review of mobile-phone data collection in developing countries examines its design lessons, and voice-forum and voice-based literacy systems such as Sangeet Swara mention it when surveying IVR precedents. The engagement is mostly brief, a supporting citation in related-work sections, but consistent: the paper serves as the cautionary datum on touchtone interfaces for first-time users.
moritz:ims:2000: The framework's most direct descendants are Cool-Mem and Cool-Cache, which carry compiler-managed caching into energy-efficient embedded and multimedia processors. In the wider literature FlexCache figures as the software-managed pole of the scratch-pad memory debate: work on static and dynamic scratch-pad allocation positions its schemes against the framework's virtualized caching, one such allocator takes it as a baseline, and the textbook Memory Systems: Cache, DRAM, Disk records it in surveying alternatives to hardware caches. The remaining citations are brief mentions in the compiler-managed memory literature — a small record, but one anchored in the community that debated how software should manage on-chip memory.
soule:debs:2013: Reception of the relaxation is modest and comes mostly by way of example. Stream-language work cites the paper when cataloguing how systems handle dynamic rates: the SPL language description and the River intermediate language discuss its hybrid scheduling, LaminarIR positions its compile-time queues against it, and work on mapping streaming applications to multi-CPU and GPU processors lists it among scheduling approaches.
